newsitem.title: GERMANY: German jobless to rise, GDP to shrink, analysts say.
newsitem.headline: German jobless to rise, GDP to shrink, analysts say.

text.p: Germany is expected to report a further rise in record unemployment and weak fourth quarter economic data this week, but there is almost no chance of the Bundesbank cutting interest rates soon, analysts said on Tuesday.

A poll of 10 economists conducted by Reuters showed most expected gross domestic product to shrink a seasonally adjusted 0.1 or 0.2 percent in the final quarter of 1996 compared with the third quarter.
February unemployment was seen on average rising about 20,000 from January's seasonally adjusted 4.317 million.

Yet all 10 of the economists polled expected the central bank to hold its discount and Lombard rates steady at 2.50 percent and 4.50 percent respectively at a regular meeting of its policy-making council on Thursday.
The three percent securities repurchase rate -- the bank's main money market rate -- was also seen on hold.
Economists said that even the weak economic data gave no reason for a Bundesbank interest rate cut given developments in other areas of the economy.

"The Bundesbank will not change interest rates on Thursday because the real interest rate level is very low and monetary policy is on an expansive course," said Klaus Baader at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

"Price rises have accelerated, the money supply is growing strongly, the mark is under downward pressure, U.S. interest rates are headed higher soon -- that all speaks against a rate change," he added.
After consumer prices trotted higher in the first two months of 1997 to just under two percent, economists believed the chances of a further interest rate easing in this cycle slimmed noticeably.
Indeed some are now starting to talk with conviction about an interest rate increase before the year end.
Werner Verbockett, economist at Commerzbank, said he expected a rate increase of 20-30 basis points in late summer. "The economy is stronger than it currently looks," he said.

January's record unemployment rate plunged Germany into a deep-seated gloom, with the extra strain on Bonn's coffers placing a question mark over whether Germany could rein in spending enough to enter European monetary union on time.
Germany aims to cuts its budget deficit back to 2.9 percent of gross domestic product in 1997, marginally below a reference level of three percent laid down in the Maastricht Treaty.
Bonn, and most independent economists, said from the outset that they expected unemployment to fall after the first couple of months of the year.
The Bild newspaper said unemployment would rise to 4.7 million in February from an unadjusted 4.66 million the month before, a smaller increase than previously reported.

While most economists predicted a continued rise in the data in February, they also warned that one major special factor which had aggravated January's data would be less of an influence in February -- the bad weather.
But they said this would be offset by continued poor orders in the key construction industry.

"Weak demand in the construction sector means that we expect the jobless figures to rise by 20,000, regardless of the developments with the weather," said Thomas Kull at Westdeutsche Landesbank in Dusseldorf.
